name: Colin Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a team lead in purchasing at a big frozen food factory on the edge of town, the one that makes ready meals for the supermarkets. My team of five buys packaging, spices and cleaning supplies, everything except the meat and veg, which a senior team handles. I got the lead role in spring when my old boss moved to the head office. A normal day is checking stock reports, placing orders, haggling with suppliers on the phone and sorting out when a delivery's late and the line might stop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's it like being the boss so young?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Odd. Two of my team are older than my dad, and they know suppliers I've never met. I'm still learning to negotiate, honestly, I fold too quickly. I live with my girlfriend Anna, who's a dental nurse, and we're saving for a deposit, but at this rate it'll take about ten years, so mostly we just pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, there's always some new thing that's meant to change everything. At work I'd say the computer's handy for the boring orders and leave it there. With my mates at the pub I'd probably make a joke of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be careful. Some of my team's work is placing the same reorders every week, and even a basic tool can do that. The factory's had two years of flat sales, so if there's a way to save one wage, they'll find it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at it and try to get better at negotiating, maybe the purchasing course my old boss did. Once a couple of the other teams use the AI reorder tool, I'd try it too. And we'd keep plugging away at the deposit, even if it's small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mainly about money and the factory being flat. Nothing to lose sleep over, but it's there. Rent goes up every year and my pay doesn't keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the deposit money come from right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hundred a month, when we can. Anna does extra Saturday clinics, I do nothing extra, which I feel bad about. My uncle keeps offering me weekend work with his heating firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you taken him up on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, a bit, and tiredness. After a week of suppliers, the last thing I want is to be under someone's boiler on a Saturday. But a heating job is honest money, and it's a trade.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because there's always some new thing.
I'd make a **joke of it** with mates at the pub.
think: Weekly **reorders** are easy for even a basic tool.
With **flat sales**, the factory will find a way to save a wage.
do: Take the **purchasing course** to get better at negotiating.
Try the **AI reorder tool** once other teams are using it.
Keep saving **a hundred a month** for the deposit.
feel: A bit uneasy about **money and flat sales**.
S0.quote: After a week of suppliers, the last thing I want is to be under someone's boiler on a Saturday. But a heating job is honest money, and it's a trade.
fieldNote: He's already under pressure from **flat sales** and rent before AI.
His uncle's **heating firm** is a fallback he's been avoiding.
He'd adopt AI tools **once others have**, a steady pattern.

steps.text: Sign up for the purchasing negotiation course his old boss took
Try the AI reorder tool once two other teams use it
Keep putting a hundred a month toward a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying is going to change, and the smart thing is to learn the new tools before you're told to. At work I'd say that to the older two, gently. With my family I'd say the factory still needs someone who knows the suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, buying is right there on the card, so purchasing will shrink. Five people becomes two or three, and the senior team could swallow us. I'm junior, so I'm not the one they'd fight for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI ordering tools properly once the senior team rolls them out, so I'm useful. I'd take my uncle up on Saturday work with his heating firm, to see if I could stick it. And we'd put the deposit on hold and build a proper emergency fund instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not a disaster yet, but I'd feel the ground moving. Anna would say I go quiet when I'm worried, and she'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Anna about the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the house waits a couple of years. Anna (my girlfriend, a dental nurse) wants a garden for a dog, and I'd feel like I was letting her down. But I'd rather rent than get a mortgage and lose my purchasing job the year after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brian, who's sixty-one and three years off his pension. Brian (the oldest buyer on my team) knows every supplier by first name. I'd want the company to let him finish properly.

say: I'd say learn the **new tools** before you're told to.
I'd tell family the factory still needs someone who **knows suppliers**.
think: **Buying** is right on the card, so purchasing will shrink.
Five could become **two or three**, and nobody would fight for a junior.
do: Learn the **AI ordering tools** once the senior team rolls them out.
Do **Saturday work** with my uncle's heating firm.
Pause the deposit and build an **emergency fund** instead.
feel: Anxious, feeling the **ground moving** and going quiet.
S1.quote: I'd rather rent than get a mortgage and lose my purchasing job the year after.
fieldNote: He knows **buying** is directly in line and that juniors go first.
The **uncle's heating firm** becomes a real test, not just an offer.
Pausing the **house deposit** weighs on him because of Anna.

steps.text: Learn the AI ordering tools as the senior team rolls them out
Work Saturdays at his uncle's heating firm for six months
Pause the house deposit and build three months' emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, and people should get a trade if they can. At work I'd keep my head down. I wouldn't be one for marches or petitions, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, purchasing is all thinking work, so it's gone by 2028. Heating and plumbing is hands-on, so robots don't come for it until around 2031. That three years is the whole reason I'd move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle for a full apprenticeship straight away, even on apprentice pay. Anna and I would cut everything, the car included if we had to, and I'd sell my motorbike. If money got too tight, we'd move in with her parents for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Apprentice pay is about half what I earn now, and Anna's job would be carrying us. I'd feel I'd failed at being the steady one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really switch with only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, because staying is worse. Uncle Pete (my uncle, a heating engineer) says it takes three years to be decent at the trade. That's exactly the gap before robots, so it's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe the robots need people to install and fix them, maybe not. I'd be thirty-two and starting again again, which is a horrible thought.

say: I'd say it'll be rough and people should **get a trade**.
I'd **keep my head down**, not march or sign petitions.
think: Purchasing is **thinking work**, so it's gone by 2028.
Heating work gets **three more years** until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Ask my uncle for a **full apprenticeship** straight away.
Sell the **motorbike** and cut everything else.
Move in with **Anna's parents** if money gets too tight.
feel: Alarmed about **half pay**, and feeling he's failed as the steady one.
S2.quote: Uncle Pete (my uncle, a heating engineer) says it takes three years to be decent at the trade. That's exactly the gap before robots, so it's tight.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot delay** precisely, matching it to apprenticeship length.
Taking **half pay** feels like personal failure to him.
His safety net is **family**: an uncle's firm and Anna's parents.

steps.text: Start a full heating apprenticeship with his uncle's firm
Sell the motorbike and cancel the gym
Move in with Anna's (his girlfriend's) parents for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for a lad to learn a trade properly. At work I'd tell the younger ones the same. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job still goes in 2031, but now I can do it in order. Keep the purchasing wage for a year or two, do the heating apprenticeship part-time, then switch. That's actually a decent plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd keep my job, use the AI ordering tools so I look useful, and do Saturdays plus one evening with Uncle Pete. I'd do the gas safety course at college. And we'd keep saving, because a bit of cushion would make the switch less scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's manageable. It's a plan with steps, which I like. I just need to not get comfortable and let the five years slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you slip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting a pay rise at the factory, honestly. If they bumped me up, I'd think why leave. Anna would have to remind me what we agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change the house plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd rent a bit longer and buy once I'm qualified. Better to buy a house as a heating engineer than as a buyer who might be gone next year. It's a slower dream, but a safer one.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **learn a trade** properly.
I'd tell the **younger ones** at work the same.
think: My job still goes in **2031**, but now I can switch in order.
A **part-time apprenticeship** first, then a full switch, is a decent plan.
do: Keep the job and use the **AI ordering tools** to look useful.
Do **Saturdays and an evening** with my uncle's firm.
Take the **gas safety course** at college.
feel: Anxious but **manageable**, with a plan in steps.
S3.quote: Better to buy a house as a heating engineer than as a buyer who might be gone next year. It's a slower dream, but a safer one.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **sequence** the switch without losing pay.
He admits a **pay rise** could tempt him to stay too long.
He'd delay the **house purchase** until he's qualified.

steps.text: Use the AI ordering tools daily at the factory
Take the gas safety course at the local college
Work Saturdays and one evening at Uncle Pete's (his uncle's) firm
Rent longer and buy a house only after qualifying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who can't sort themselves out in a decade isn't trying. That's what I'd say down the pub, anyway. At work I'd say keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably stay in purchasing a good while, maybe move up a level. Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven when it goes, and I could switch to heating in my early thirties. I'd have options, which is a nice feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job, take the purchasing course, and use the AI tools as they become normal. I'd do weekend work with Uncle Pete for a couple of years to learn the trade slowly. And we'd buy a small house in about five years, once there's a bit saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but fine. It's the rent and the deposit that bother me day to day, not the robots. Ten years is normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who can't sort themselves out isn't trying. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. Anyone who can't sort themselves out in a decade isn't trying. I said that at the pub, but Brian (the oldest buyer on my team) wouldn't have the same chances. Brian's sixty-one. So maybe not everyone, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Anna say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we should get a dog and stop worrying. Anna's job as a dental nurse is hands-on, so she's not too fussed. She's the calm one.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty for anyone trying.
I'd tell people at work to **keep learning** while there's time.
think: I could stay in purchasing a while and **move up a level**.
I could switch to **heating** in my early thirties, which gives me options.
do: Take the **purchasing course** and use AI tools as they become normal.
Learn the trade slowly with **weekend work** for two years.
Buy a **small house** in about five years.
feel: Uneasy but fine, with **rent and the deposit** as the daily worry.
S4.quote: Anyone who can't sort themselves out in a decade isn't trying. I said that at the pub, but Brian (the oldest buyer on my team) wouldn't have the same chances.
fieldNote: He catches himself on the **pub line** and softens it for older workers.
Ten years gives him **options**, which settles him.
His partner's **hands-on job** keeps the household calm.

steps.text: Use the new AI ordering tools as they become standard
Work weekends with Uncle Pete (his uncle) to learn heating
Save toward a small house deposit over five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to go to apprentice pay overnight and Anna would carry us. What would help is apprenticeships that pay a proper wage for people my age, and employers giving notice early. Not handouts, just a fair chance to learn a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what younger blokes like me feel about being carried by a partner. Being carried by a partner isn't supposed to matter these days, but it does. I'd want to be pulling my weight.

headlineQuote: Being carried by a partner isn't supposed to matter these days, but it does. I'd want to be pulling my weight.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old purchasing team lead** at a frozen food factory, managing five buyers.
He lives with Anna, a **dental nurse**, and they're slowly saving for a house deposit.
His uncle runs a **heating firm**, which becomes his fallback in every fast scenario.
He's steady: he'd use AI once proven and **plan in steps** with more time.
He values **pulling his weight**, and apprentice pay feels like failure to him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which forces him onto apprentice pay with Anna carrying them.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for people his age, at a proper wage.
Employers giving **early notice** rather than handouts.
